paragraphs: “As for him, the hound does not even dare to look me in the face. I will not sit in council with him, and I will have no share in any plan of his. He has wronged and deceived me enough. He will not cheat me a second time. Let him go his own way, since Zeus has taken away his reason. I hate his presents, and I do not care a straw for the man himself. Let him offer ten times what he has offered now, or twenty—no, not even if he gave me everything he owns in the world, now or ever. Let him promise me the wealth of Orchomenus or of Egyptian Thebes, the richest city in the whole world, which has a hundred gates, and through each gate two hundred men can drive out at once with their chariots and horses. Let him offer gifts as many as the sands of the sea or the dust of the plain. Even so he will not move me until I have paid him back in full for the bitter wrong he did me. I will not marry his daughter. She could be as beautiful as Aphrodite and as skilled as Athena, and I would still have none of her. Let some other man take her, one who suits her better and rules a larger kingdom. If the gods bring me safely home, Peleus himself will find me a wife. There are Achaean women in Hellas and Phthia, daughters of kings who rule cities, and I can take whichever of them I like and marry her. Many times, back home in Phthia, I longed to court a wife who would suit me and to enjoy the riches my old father Peleus had won. My life is worth more to me than all the wealth of Ilium in the days when it was at peace, before the Achaeans came, or than all the treasure that lies on the stone floor of Apollo’s temple under the cliffs of Pytho. Cattle and sheep can be won by raiding, and a man can buy tripods and horses if he wants them. But once a man’s life has left him, it can be neither bought nor raided back.

“My mother Thetis tells me that death can come to me in one of two ways. If I stay here and fight, I will not get home alive, but my name will live forever. If I go home, my name will die, but I will live a long time before death takes me. To the rest of you I say, ‘Go home. You will never take Ilium.’ Zeus has held his hand over the city to protect it, and its people have taken heart. So go, as is your duty, and give the princes of the Achaeans the message I am sending. Tell them to find some other plan to save their ships and their people, because the one they have settled on now will not work while my anger lasts. As for Phoenix, let him sleep here, so that he can sail home with me in the morning if he wishes. But I will not take him by force.”

They all stayed silent, shaken by how harshly he had refused them. At last the old knight Phoenix, in his great fear for the ships of the Achaeans, burst into tears and spoke. “Noble Achilles, if you are really set on going home, and your fierce anger will not let you do anything to save the ships from burning, then how can I stay here without you, my son? Your father Peleus sent me with you on the day he sent you from Phthia to Agamemnon, when you were only a boy. You knew nothing yet of war, or of the skills that make men known in council. He sent me to train you in every excellence of speech and action. So, my son, I will not stay here without you—no, not even if heaven itself were to strip the years from me and make me as young as I was when I first left Hellas, the land of fair women. I was running from the anger of my father Amyntor, son of Ormenus. He was furious with me over his concubine, whom he loved to the wrong of his wife, my mother. My mother begged me without stopping to sleep with the woman myself, so that she would come to hate my father, and in time I gave in. But my father soon found out, and cursed me bitterly, calling the dreadful Erinyes to witness. He prayed that no son of mine would ever sit on his knees—and the gods, Zeus of the world below and awful Proserpine, fulfilled his curse. I made up my mind to kill him, but some god held back my rashness. He made me think of what men’s evil tongues would say, and how I would be branded the murderer of my father. Even so, I could not bear to stay in my father’s house with him so bitter against me. My cousins and kinsmen gathered around me and pressed me hard to stay. They slaughtered many sheep and many oxen, set many fat hogs to roast before the fire, and broached many jars of my father’s wine. For nine whole nights they set a guard over me, taking turns to watch, and they kept a fire burning always, both in the cloister of the outer court and in the inner court at the doors of the room where I lay. But when the darkness of the tenth night came, I broke through the closed doors of my room, after slipping quickly and unseen through the guards and the women servants, and I climbed the wall of the outer court. Then I fled through Hellas until I came to fertile Phthia, mother of sheep, and to King Peleus. He welcomed me and treated me as a father treats an only son who will inherit all his wealth. He made me rich and put me over many people, setting me on the borders of Phthia, where I ruled as chief over the Dolopians.

“It was I, Achilles, who made you what you are. I loved you with all my heart. You would not eat at home, or anywhere else you went, until I had set you on my knees, cut up the tasty morsel for you, and held the wine cup to your lips. Many times you dribbled your wine over my shirt in a baby’s helplessness. I had endless trouble with you. But I knew that heaven had given me no child of my own, so I made a son of you, Achilles, so that in my hour of need you would protect me. Now I tell you: fight your pride and beat it. Do not nurse your anger forever. The might and majesty of heaven are greater than ours, and even heaven can be appeased. When a man has sinned, he prays to the gods and wins them back with his pitiful cries, with frankincense, with drink offerings and the smell of burnt sacrifice. For prayers are like daughters of great Zeus. They are lame and wrinkled, and they squint, and they follow in the footsteps of sin. Sin is fierce and swift-footed, so it leaves them far behind, and, a curse to mankind always, it outruns them to the ends of the world. Still, the prayers come limping after, and heal what sin has done. If a man respects these daughters of Zeus when they come near him, they bless him and listen to his prayers as well. But if he refuses them and will not listen, they go to Zeus the son of Cronus and pray that sin will overtake him, so that he comes to regret it bitterly. So, Achilles, give these daughters of Zeus the reverence they are due, and bow before them as all good men bow. If the son of Atreus were not offering you gifts and promising more later—if he were still furious and unyielding—I would not be the one to tell you to throw off your anger and help the Achaeans, however great their need. But he is giving much now, and will give more later. He has sent his captains to plead for him, and chosen the men who are dearest to you of all the Argives. Do not make their words and their coming useless. Until now your anger was justified. We have heard in song how heroes of old quarreled when fury seized them, yet gifts could still win them over, and fair words could soothe them.

“I have an old story in my mind—a very old one—but you are all friends, so I will tell it. The Curetes and the Aetolians were fighting and killing one another around Calydon, the Aetolians defending the city and the Curetes trying to destroy it. Artemis of the golden throne was angry and did them harm, because Oeneus had not offered her the first fruits of his harvest. The other gods had all been feasted with great sacrifices, but to the daughter of great Zeus alone he had made no sacrifice. He had forgotten her, or somehow it had slipped his mind, and this was a grievous sin. In her anger the archer goddess sent a monstrous creature against him, a savage wild boar with great white tusks. It did great harm to his orchard lands, uprooting apple trees in full bloom and flinging them to the ground. But Meleager son of Oeneus gathered huntsmen and hounds from many cities and killed it. The boar was so huge that not a few men were needed, and it laid many a man on his funeral pyre. Then the goddess set the Curetes and the Aetolians fighting furiously over the boar’s head and skin.

“As long as Meleager was in the field, things went badly for the Curetes, and for all their numbers they could not hold their ground under the city walls. But in time Meleager grew angry, as even a wise man sometimes will. He was enraged at his mother Althaea, and so he stayed at home with his wedded wife, fair Cleopatra. She was the daughter of Marpessa daughter of Euenus, and of Ides, the man who was then alive. This Ides took up his bow and faced King Apollo himself for the sake of fair Marpessa. After that, her father and mother named her Alcyone, because her mother had cried out in grief like the halcyon bird when Phoebus Apollo carried her off. So Meleager stayed at home with Cleopatra, feeding the anger he felt over his mother’s curses. His mother was grieving for her brother’s death. She prayed to the gods and beat the earth with her hands, calling on Hades and on awful Proserpine. She was on her knees, and her bosom was wet with tears, as she prayed that they would kill her son. And Erinys, who walks in darkness and knows no pity, heard her from Erebus.

“Soon the din of battle was heard around the gates of Calydon, and the dull thud of battering against the walls. The elders of the Aetolians begged Meleager. They sent the most important of their priests to ask him to come out and help them, and promised him a great reward. They told him to choose fifty plow-gates in the most fertile part of the plain of Calydon, half of it vineyard and half open plowland. The old warrior Oeneus pleaded with him, standing at the threshold of his room and beating on the doors in supplication. His sisters and his mother herself begged him hard, but he refused them all the more. Those of his comrades who were nearest and dearest to him prayed to him too, but they could not move him. That went on until the foe was battering at the very doors of his chamber, and the Curetes had scaled the walls and were setting fire to the city. Then at last his sorrowing wife described to him the horrors that fall on people whose city is taken. She reminded him how the men are slain, and the city is given over to the flames, while the women and children are carried off into captivity. When he heard all this, his heart was touched, and he put on his armor and went out. So he saved the city of the Aetolians of his own free will. But they no longer gave him any of the rich rewards they had offered before, and though he saved the city he gained nothing by it. Do not let yourself think this way, my son. Do not let heaven lure you into any such course. When the ships are burning, it will be harder to save them. Take the gifts and go, for then the Achaeans will honor you like a god. But if you fight without taking them, you may beat the battle back, but you will not be held in the same honor.”

And Achilles answered, “Phoenix, old friend and father, I have no need of that kind of honor. I have honor from Zeus himself, and it will stay with me at my ships as long as I have breath in my body and strength in my limbs. And I tell you this—take it to heart—stop upsetting me with this weeping and lamenting for the sake of the son of Atreus. If you love him so well, you may lose the love I bear you. You should rather help me trouble those who trouble me. Be king as much as I am, and share equal honor with me. The others will carry back my answer. You stay here yourself and sleep comfortably in your bed, and at daybreak we will decide whether to stay or go.”

Then he nodded quietly to Patroclus, as a sign that he should prepare a bed for Phoenix and that the others should leave. Ajax son of Telamon spoke next. “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, let us go. I can see that our journey is useless. We must take our answer, unwelcome as it is, to the Danaans, who are waiting for it. Achilles is savage and without mercy. He is cruel, and cares nothing for the love his comrades gave him more than all the others. He is unforgiving. Yet when a man’s brother or son has been killed, he will accept a payment as compensation from the killer, and the wrongdoer, having paid in full, stays in peace among his own people. But you, Achilles—the gods have put a wicked, unforgiving spirit in your heart, and all this over one single girl, when we are now offering you the seven best we have, and much else besides. Be more gracious, and respect the hospitality of your own roof. We are here with you as messengers from the host of the Danaans, and we would gladly be held nearest and dearest to you of all the Achaeans.”

“Ajax,” replied Achilles, “noble son of Telamon, what you have said pleases me well. But my blood boils when I think it over and remember how the son of Atreus treated me with contempt, as if I were some vile tramp, and in front of the Argives too. So go and deliver your message. Say that I will have nothing to do with fighting until Hector, son of noble Priam, reaches the tents of the Myrmidons in his murderous course and throws fire on their ships. For all his lust for battle, I think he will be held back once he is at my own tent and ship.”

After that, each man took his double cup, made his drink offering, and went back to the ships, with Odysseus leading the way. Patroclus told his men and the maidservants to make a comfortable bed for Phoenix, and they did, with sheepskins, a rug, and a sheet of fine linen. The old man lay down and waited for morning. Achilles slept in an inner room, and beside him lay the daughter of Phorbas, lovely Diomede, whom he had carried off from Lesbos. Patroclus lay on the other side of the room, and with him fair Iphis, whom Achilles had given him when he took Scyros, the city of Enyeus.

When the envoys reached the tents of the son of Atreus, the Achaeans rose, raised cups of gold to them, and began to question them. King Agamemnon was the first. “Tell me, Odysseus,” he said, “will he save the ships from burning, or did he refuse, and is he still furious?”

Odysseus answered, “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, Achilles will not be calmed. He is angrier than ever, and he rejects both you and your gifts. He tells you to take counsel with the Achaeans and save the ships and the host as best you can. As for himself, he said that at daybreak he would drag his ships down into the water. He also said he would advise everyone to sail home too, because you will never reach your goal of Ilium. ‘Zeus,’ he said, ‘has laid his hand over the city to protect it, and its people have taken heart.’ That is what he said, and the others who were with me can tell you the same story: Ajax and the two heralds, both men who can be trusted. The old man Phoenix stayed where he was to sleep, because Achilles wanted it so, to let him go home with him in the morning if he wished. But Achilles will not take him by force.”

They all stayed silent, sitting for a long time quiet and downcast at how harshly Achilles had refused them. At last Diomedes spoke. “Most noble son of Atreus, Agamemnon, king of men, you should not have pleaded with the son of Peleus or offered him gifts. He is proud enough already, and you have pushed him further into his pride. Let him stay or go as he wishes. He will fight later, when he is in the mood and heaven puts it in his mind. Now let us all do as I say. We have eaten and drunk our fill, so let us rest, for in rest there is both strength and support. But when fair rosy-fingered Dawn appears, bring your host and your horsemen out in front of the ships at once, urging them on, and fight yourself among the foremost.”
So he spoke, and the other chieftains approved his words. They made their drink offerings, and each man went to his own tent, where they lay down and enjoyed the gift of sleep.
